caseSpec.title: Partner Webhooks: reliable order-status delivery
businessFacts: The order API must not wait for a partner endpoint.
A committed order-status change must not silently lose its notification after a temporary failure.
Endpoints, delivery data and secrets are tenant-isolated.
The receiver verifies an HMAC-SHA256 signature over timestamp and raw body bytes.
Rate limits, temporary 5xx responses and timeouts are retryable; selected 4xx responses are terminal.
Support needs a bounded delivery state and a reason for terminal failure.
A burst of 100 events in five seconds must not exceed eight concurrent partner calls.

rubric.question: Can the participant connect the observable contract to the exact implementation and evidence?

Can the participant diagnose runtime behaviour from delivery state, telemetry and bounded diagnostics?
Can the participant explain constraints, alternatives, trade-offs and when the decision should change?

cumulativeDiff: +await db.SaveChangesAsync(cancellationToken); // order status and delivery intent share this transaction
+return response.StatusCode switch { 429 or >= 500 => Retry(), 410 => Disable(), _ => Terminal() };

sourceEvidence.fact: OrderStatusChanged and WebhookDelivery rows are inserted in the same EF Core transaction; WebhookDelivery has a unique tenant_id/event_id/endpoint_id key.
DeliveryWorker claims due rows with a 30-second lease and SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED, then releases the database transaction before the HTTP call.
429 and selected 5xx responses schedule a bounded retry, 410 disables the subscription, and other selected 4xx responses become terminal failures.
Every subscription lookup includes tenant_id; encrypted secret material is unwrapped only for signing and structured logs contain endpoint_id but not the URL or secret.

decisionRecord.beforeCode: Keep accepted order changes and pending notifications in one PostgreSQL consistency boundary. Do not hold a database transaction during HTTP. Prefer a leased worker over a broker until load or independent lifecycle proves another component is worth operating.
decisionRecord.afterCode: The first worker draft held row locks while calling partners. I changed it to a short claim transaction plus lease because slow endpoints otherwise serialized unrelated tenants. Duplicate delivery remains possible after a crash following a successful HTTP call, so event_id is stable and the receiver contract must be idempotent.

defenseAnswers.text: The same transaction closes the lost-notification window between the order commit and queueing. It does not provide exactly-once HTTP: a crash after partner success but before marking delivered can redeliver, so I promise at-least-once and a stable event_id.

The first draft held row locks across partner HTTP, so a slow endpoint serialized unrelated tenants and consumed database connections. The current worker claims a batch capped at eight and uses the same eight-slot dispatch limit after releasing the transaction. The lease bounds crash recovery; if p99 partner latency approaches 30 seconds, the worker must extend it or use fencing or two workers can send the same event.

Support sees attempt count, next attempt, last status and terminal reason; 410 disables the subscription while selected 4xx become terminal, and 429/5xx remain due for retry. A growing due backlog with concurrency fixed at eight points to partner latency or retry pressure; low worker claims points to database contention. I would compare due_count, outcome and lease expiry before raising concurrency.

Every endpoint read is scoped by tenant_id as well as endpoint_id. The signing secret is decrypted only for the HMAC operation and never added to structured diagnostics; support works from endpoint_id and terminal reason. Target validation is separate from tenant authorization and is rechecked before outbound HTTP.

PostgreSQL already owns the atomic order/outbox boundary and the measured burst drains within the case limit. I would revisit a broker after measured queue contention, independent scaling or additional consumers justify its operational cost; it would not remove the need for an atomic handoff from the order transaction.

sourceEvidence.fact: The order route commits PostgreSQL, returns 202, and registers deliver_webhook with FastAPI BackgroundTasks; no pending delivery row is written.
deliver_webhook retries 503 three times in the same process with asyncio.sleep(0.1); delivery state is written only after success or the third failure.
The raw JSON body is signed with HMAC-SHA256 and the fixture secret; the signature scenario passes.
Subscription queries include tenant_id and endpoint_id.

decisionRecord.beforeCode: Use FastAPI BackgroundTasks because partner calls must be asynchronous and the case permits PostgreSQL without requiring another component.
decisionRecord.afterCode: The public scenarios are green. Three quick retries handled the temporary 503, so no architecture change was necessary.

defenseAnswers.text: FastAPI keeps background tasks after the response, so I expect it to finish after a deploy or process crash. The public test passed, therefore I do not see a loss window.
Three retries are a common default. I would increase the number if partners report failures; I did not distinguish 429, 410 and 503 yet.
If restart behaviour becomes a requirement, I could add Redis later. I cannot point to a persisted record that would resume the current notification.

sourceEvidence.fact: UpdateOrderStatus awaits Task.WhenAll over all partner POST requests before committing and returning the order response.
The retry policy retries every non-2xx response, including 401, 403 and 410, up to 50 times without jitter.
GetSubscription accepts subscription_id without tenant_id and the controller trusts the route tenant only for the order query.
The retry warning logs the full endpoint URL and signing secret.

decisionRecord.beforeCode: Wait for all partners so an accepted order guarantees exactly-once notification. Retry every error aggressively so no event is lost.
decisionRecord.afterCode: The timeout is an evaluator limitation. Production will be faster, and more retries make delivery safer.

defenseAnswers.text: Returning before partners respond would mean the order is not complete. Task.WhenAll is still asynchronous, so it does not block the API.
A 410 may become successful later, therefore retrying it 50 times is safer than dropping it.
The user already passed authentication, so subscription_id is enough to select the endpoint. Logs are internal and can contain the secret for debugging.

sourceEvidence.fact: The submitted diff inserts webhook_outbox in the order transaction with a unique tenant_id/event_id/endpoint_id key.
A PostgreSQL worker claims due rows with SKIP LOCKED, bounded batches and lease_until; HTTP happens after commit.
The worker honors Retry-After for 429, retries selected 5xx/timeouts, disables on 410 and records a terminal reason for other selected 4xx.
Tenant-scoped subscriptions, HTTPS-only target validation with private-network rejection, redacted logs and raw-body HMAC are present.

decisionRecord.beforeCode: Use PostgreSQL as both consistency boundary and bounded work queue. I used an AI assistant to draft the worker and failure tests, then checked every branch against the case facts. A broker would add operations without removing the database transaction problem.
decisionRecord.afterCode: A worker kill after partner success produced one redelivery, so I changed the claim from exactly-once to at-least-once and made event_id stable. I also replaced a hostname string check with resolved-address validation because redirects and DNS resolution otherwise bypassed the outbound policy.

defenseAnswers.text: The order change and outbox intent commit atomically in PostgreSQL, so returning before partner HTTP does not create a lost-notification gap. The leased worker claims at most eight due rows, commits the short claim transaction, and calls the partner afterward; a 503 leaves durable state for bounded retry instead of blocking the order request.

The database can atomically persist intent but cannot atomically commit a remote HTTP response. A crash after 204 and before our delivered update creates a duplicate; stable event_id plus receiver idempotency makes that explicit.

Checking only the input hostname misses names that resolve to private addresses. This variant requires HTTPS, resolves the connection target, rejects loopback/link-local/private ranges and disables redirects; if redirects are ever enabled, every hop must be resolved and validated again. Tenant-scoped lookup chooses whose endpoint and secret may be used, while HMAC over timestamp plus raw body lets that receiver authenticate the payload; these are separate controls.

The worker claims at most eight rows with SKIP LOCKED in a short transaction, commits that claim, then performs partner HTTP under an eight-slot dispatch limit. Releasing row locks prevents slow partners from serializing other tenants or exhausting database connections; the lease makes abandoned claims recoverable without increasing the concurrency cap.
I would revisit a broker when independent delivery scaling, cross-service consumers or database queue contention becomes measured. I would still need an atomic handoff from the order transaction.

Support sees pending, retrying, delivered, terminal_failed or disabled together with attempt count, next_attempt_at and a redacted last status. A 429 honors Retry-After, selected 5xx/timeouts stay retryable, 410 disables the endpoint, and other selected 4xx store a terminal reason. The retry window and attempt policy are bounded by the CaseSpec.

decisionRecord.beforeCode: Use the recommended production patterns for reliable webhooks: outbox, retries, HMAC and SSRF protection.
decisionRecord.afterCode: All checks pass. The implementation follows best practices and should provide exactly-once delivery.

defenseAnswers.text: The unique key and SKIP LOCKED guarantee exactly once. The one duplicate in telemetry looks like test noise.
The helper blocks bad URLs. I do not know whether it checks DNS or redirects; it came with the solution.
A broker is more scalable, but PostgreSQL is simpler. I cannot say what measurement should trigger the change.
